regions.label: The nine NASA candidate regions
regions.rule: the cell is one of the 280 cells of the nine candidate landing regions NASA announced on 28 October 2024 (the Lunar base zone)

regions.label: South-polar region outside the nine NASA regions
regions.rule: latitude at or below 75 degrees south, not in A

regions.label: North-polar region
regions.rule: latitude at or above 75 degrees north

regions.label: Low equatorial plains (the maria)
regions.rule: within 30 degrees of the equator and elevation at or below -1,200 m (the Solar panels zone)

regions.label: Far side
regions.rule: longitude more than 90 degrees from the central meridian (far side), not in A to D

regions.label: Near-side highlands and mid-latitudes (includes the northern maria beyond 30 degrees)
regions.rule: every other cell: near side (longitude within 90 degrees of the central meridian), between 75 S and 75 N, outside the low equatorial plains

texts.general_note: Spacecraft have landed in many parts of the Moon: Apollo and Luna near the equator, Chang'e 4 and 6 on the far side, IM-2 near the south pole. Each test is searched in one zone the team chose; other regions are explained, not ruled out.

zone_why.rover: Why the south pole: our rover test follows NASA's plans there, such as the VIPER rover, meant to map water ice in permanently shadowed craters. It is not the best match by terrain: in our data the north pole pairs about as many Earth sites (9,888 against 10,192) and more closely (median slope gap 0.10° against 0.41°).
zone_why.solar: Why the equatorial maria: we target a high Sun on the lowest, flattest plains (median slope 1.1°), where Apollo landed, with sunlight as high as anywhere in our data: about 10 kWh/m² a day (highlands: 8 to 9). Nearly every Earth site without a twin here would have one in the highlands. Flat polar ground gets at most 2.48, below the 3.54 our sites need.
zone_why.lunar_base: Why NASA's nine regions: our base test follows NASA's crew-landing plan, which named nine candidate regions near the south pole in October 2024. This is the team's choice, not a physical limit. Each pair is a likeness of thermal position (how cold and how variable a place is within its own world), not of temperature; the real difference is shown with every pair.

rover.C: Not our rover zone, but our data do not rule it out: by terrain the north pole matches Earth sites as closely or more (median similarity 99.7 against 93.3 in our south-pole zone). Our rover test follows NASA's south-pole plans, such as VIPER, for water ice. NASA's GRAIL probes ended their mission here in 2012.
rover.D: Rovers have driven here, like Lunokhod 2 in 1973. Our rover test is about finding water ice, as NASA plans with VIPER, and NASA says that ice lies at the poles, in permanently shadowed areas, so we search near the south pole.
rover.E: China's Yutu-2 rover drove here after Chang'e 4 landed in 2019, so rovers work on the far side. Our rover test targets polar water ice, like NASA's VIPER, and far-side missions also need a relay satellite to talk to Earth.
rover.F: Rovers have worked here: Lunokhod 1, China's Yutu and India's Pragyan, which reached 69° S in 2023 on what India calls a south-pole landing. Our rover test follows NASA's VIPER plan for water ice in permanently shadowed craters, so the team set its zone at 75° S and beyond.

solar.A: Near the pole the Sun stays low: in our data no flat ground beyond 75° S gets more than 2.48 kWh/m² a day, and even our least sunny Earth site would need 3.54 for a twin. Some ridges stay lit most of the year, suiting vertical panels, a different test. IM-2 landed here in 2025.
solar.B: IM-1 landed here in 2024, and spots on Shackleton's rim are jointly lit over 90% of the year. But for a flat panel the Sun stays low: in our data no flat ground beyond 75° S gets more than 2.48 kWh/m² a day, below the 3.54 our least sunny Earth site would need.
solar.C: The Sun stays near the horizon here: in our data no flat ground beyond 75° N gets more than 2.45 kWh/m² a day, below the 3.54 our least sunny Earth site would need for a twin. Our panel test is designed for a high Sun on flat ground, so we search the maria.
solar.E: Our data do not rule this region out: 18,776 of our 18,777 Earth sites would find a sunlight twin here, including 12,416 with none in the maria. Chang'e 4 and 6 landed here. The team chose the maria as its design target: more sunlight on average (about 10 vs 9 kWh/m² a day) on lower, flatter plains.
solar.F: Our data do not rule this region out: 18,776 of our 18,777 Earth sites would find a sunlight twin here, including 12,416 with none in the maria. Apollo 14 and 16, SLIM and Chang'e 3 and 5 landed here. The team chose the maria as its design target: more sunlight on average (about 10 vs 8 kWh/m² a day) on lower, flatter plains.

lunar_base.B: IM-1 landed here in 2024, and more robotic missions target the south-polar region. Our base test follows NASA's plan for its first Artemis crew landing, Artemis IV, so it uses only the nine candidate regions NASA named in October 2024. This is the team's choice, not a physical limit.
lunar_base.C: NASA's crewed landing plans point to the south pole, not here, although the north pole also has cold shadowed craters. NASA's GRAIL probes ended their mission here in 2012. Our base zone is NASA's nine south-polar regions.
lunar_base.D: Apollo 11, 12, 15 and 17 landed crews here; early Apollo sites stayed near the equator for operational reasons, such as a safe return path. NASA's next crew landing, Artemis IV, targets the south pole, where shadowed areas can preserve water. We follow that.
lunar_base.E: Chang'e 4 and 6 landed here; Chang'e 6 landed with support from the Queqiao-2 relay satellite. NASA lists communication with Earth among its criteria for crew landing sites and chose nine south-polar regions; our base test uses those regions.
lunar_base.F: Apollo 14 and 16, India's Chandrayaan-3 and Japan's SLIM landed here. NASA's next crew landing, Artemis IV, targets the south pole, where shadowed areas can preserve water, in nine regions picked for lighting, terrain and Earth communication. Our base test uses them.
